html:
This dua — Rabbighfir lī wa tub ʿalayya innaka antat-Tawwābur-Raḥīm — is one of the shortest and most frequently repeated istighfār formulas in the entire corpus of the Prophet's ﷺ private worship. It consists of three Arabic verbs and three divine names, and yet Ibn ʿUmar (raḍiyAllāhu ʿanhumā) counted the Prophet ﷺ saying it a hundred times in a single sitting before he rose. The narration is in Sunan Abī Dāwūd 1516, Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 3434, Sunan Ibn Mājah 3814, and Musnad Aḥmad. Al-Tirmidhī himself graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb, and al-Albānī graded it ṣaḥīḥ in Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan Abī Dāwūd. The chain is sound by consensus of the muḥaddithūn.

What makes this short formula remarkable is not its vocabulary — every word in it appears elsewhere in the Qur'an and Sunna — but its density. In nine Arabic words it accomplishes three distinct acts of worship: (1) explicit petition for forgiveness of specific past deeds (ighfir lī, imperative request for sitr/concealment and ʿafw/pardon of sins), (2) petition for the ongoing act of divine returning (tub ʿalayya, imperative request that Allah turn toward the servant), and (3) a theological ground that explains why the first two are reasonable requests at all (innaka anta t-Tawwābu r-Raḥīm, affirmation of Allah's two most relevant names). This mirrors the structural pattern Ibn al-Qayyim identified in Madārij al-Sālikīn: the servant asks, then names Allah by the attribute that justifies the asking. One does not petition al-Qahhār for mercy by that name; one petitions al-Tawwāb for turning by that name.

Why two verbs for one apparent request?

The dua is often mistranslated as if ighfir lī and tub ʿalayya were synonymous — "forgive me and forgive me again." They are not. Ibn Taymiyyah (Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā 10/255) and Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Wābil al-Ṣayyib) both unpack the distinction at length:

  • Maghfira (from the root gh-f-r, "to cover") is Allah's act of concealing, protecting from the consequence, and removing the sin's trace from the record. It is primarily about the sin itself — its traces, its records, its effects on the Day of Judgment. One asks for maghfira regarding what one has already done.
  • Tawba (from the root t-w-b, "to return"), when attributed to Allah with the preposition ʿalā, is Allah's act of returning toward the servant with acceptance, enabling the servant's own tawba, and restoring the relationship. It is primarily about the relationship — Allah's facing-back-toward the servant who has turned. One asks for tawba regarding the state going forward.

So ighfir lī wa tub ʿalayya is a complete petition: cover what I have done, AND turn to me so that I remain able to turn to You. The Qur'an itself pairs these two acts repeatedly — Qur'an 2:160: fa-ulāʾika atūbu ʿalayhim wa anā t-Tawwābu r-Raḥīm, "those are the ones to whom I will turn, and I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful" — using the same two names that close our dua. The Prophet ﷺ was not padding the formula with a redundant verb; he was teaching the servant to ask for both the covering of what passed and the openness of what is to come.

The hundred-times number — not a magical count

Ibn ʿUmar's precise counting — fī al-majlis al-wāḥid miʾa marrā, "a hundred times in a single sitting" — has sometimes been misread as suggesting that this specific count holds a hidden virtue. Ibn Ḥajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī and al-Mubārakfūrī in Tuḥfat al-Aḥwadhī (sharḥ on al-Tirmidhī 3434) both clarify that the hundred is descriptive, not prescriptive. The Prophet ﷺ did not instruct anyone to say it a hundred times; Ibn ʿUmar is simply reporting what he observed. The point of the narration is that the Prophet ﷺ, who had no sins to seek forgiveness for, nevertheless saturated his sittings with this formula to the point that his companion counted a hundred utterances before he rose.

This observation sits inside a larger prophetic pattern recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6307 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2702, where the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, I seek forgiveness from Allah and turn to Him in repentance more than seventy times a day" — and in another narration, a hundred times. Al-Nawawī in Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn (Bāb al-Istighfār) and al-Adhkār explains that this is the single most important hermeneutical frame for understanding Prophetic istighfār: it is not an acknowledgment of sins committed. The Prophet ﷺ was maʿṣūm, protected from sin. His istighfār is the servant's response to receiving — the believer's constant return to the ground of his existence, which is Allah's prior mercy. The hundred times is not atonement arithmetic. It is the texture of a life spent facing the One who sustains it moment by moment.

The practical takeaway, as Ibn Taymiyyah frames it: do not get fixated on the hundred-count. Say the dua when you sit, when you rise, when you walk, when a conversation ends, when you catch yourself in a thought you shouldn't have had. The frequency is the sunna; the exact number is Ibn ʿUmar's testimony about one majlis.

The three divine names at the close

The dua ends with innaka anta t-Tawwābu r-Raḥīm — two divine names in apposition — plus the pronoun of emphasis anta, "You alone." Al-Qurṭubī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān (on Qur'an 2:160, which uses this exact phrasing) notes that the construction innaka anta X is one of the strongest emphatic forms in Arabic. The Qur'an uses it in moments of theological finality: Mūsā's prayer in 20:46, Ibrāhīm's in 2:127–128, and here as a divine self-description in 2:160. The believer who repeats this dua is not merely informing Allah of His own names; he is claiming the implication: "since You are the One who returns to Your servants, return to me; since You are the Merciful, show me that mercy."

Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān distinguishes Tawwāb (hyperbolic form, fawwāl) from Tāʾib: Tawwāb means the One who returns to His servants repeatedly, abundantly, as a habitual attribute. It is not that Allah turns once; it is that returning is what He does. This is why the servant can say tub ʿalayya after having fallen a hundred times. One does not exhaust Allah's turning. Al-Ṭabarī in Jāmiʿ al-Bayān (on 2:37, where Ādam himself receives Allah's turning: fa-tāba ʿalayh) grounds this in the first narrative of the human: before any human had ever sinned twice, Allah had already named Himself the One who turns. The dua places us in the lineage of Ādam — not merely a sinner, but a sinner for whom returning was built into creation itself.

Pairing Tawwāb with Raḥīm seals the formula. Ibn Kathīr in his Tafsīr (on 2:160) explains that Tawwāb addresses the past (He turns toward the one who turned) and Raḥīm addresses the future (His mercy continues to envelop the one He has accepted). The servant has not just been forgiven; he has been drawn back into the ambit of divine mercy. This is why the dua does not conclude with al-Ghafūr (the Forgiving) alone — forgiveness without ongoing mercy is a transaction. The Prophet ﷺ taught us to ask for the relationship, not just the pardon.

Where this dua sits in daily practice

Al-Nawawī in al-Adhkār and Ibn al-Qayyim in Zād al-Maʿād both place this dua in the general category of adhkār al-majālis, "the remembrances of sittings," alongside the more famous kaffārat al-majlis (subḥānaka Allāhumma wa bi-ḥamdika… from Abū Dāwūd 4859). The Prophet ﷺ did not legislate a fixed wird schedule for this formula the way he did for the morning and evening adhkār in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6306 (Sayyid al-Istighfār) or the counts after prayer in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 597 (33+33+34). This dua is more diffuse — it is for whenever one is sitting, with no upper bound.

Classical practice:

  • Many of the salaf would repeat it during the pauses in a lesson, in walking between tasks, and before standing from any formal majlis.
  • It is a natural companion to Sayyid al-Istighfār in the morning and evening: Sayyid al-Istighfār for the twice-daily, longer confession-and-tawba; this short formula for the hundred-plus micro-returnings in between.
  • Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah is reported in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā (10/254) to have continued saying this dua for the duration of a Fajr-to-Ḍuḥā sitting (roughly 90 minutes), after which he said: "This is my morning meal; if I did not take it, my strength would collapse" — a well-known report from his student Ibn al-Qayyim in Madārij al-Sālikīn. The story is less about the exact count and more about treating istighfār as spiritual nourishment that sustains the day's remaining obligations.

Pastoral honesty

Three honest clarifications, continuing the pattern of the earlier dua intros in this series:

  • This short formula is NOT a replacement for Sayyid al-Istighfār. The two serve different functions. Sayyid al-Istighfār is the theological istighfār — a sitting-down, tri-partite acknowledgment with the Paradise-upon-same-day-death clause attached to it. This short dua is the ambient istighfār — the servant's running commentary of return throughout the day. One memorizes and uses both; neither does the other's work.
  • Reciting it quickly without attention is still better than not reciting it at all. This runs against a certain modern Sufi framing that suggests mechanical dhikr has no value. Al-Nawawī in al-Adhkār and Ibn al-Qayyim in al-Wābil al-Ṣayyib both note explicitly that attentive dhikr carries greater weight — but inattentive dhikr still carries weight, is still sawāb, and training the tongue in a formula is one of the mechanisms by which the heart eventually catches up. Do not stop saying it because you are distracted; say it until you are not.
  • The dua does not guarantee instant felt-relief or emotional change. Its promises are the two Qur'anic attributes it names: Allah's turning and Allah's mercy. Whether the servant feels turned-toward in a given sitting is not something the dua pledges. The Prophet ﷺ said it a hundred times a sitting; he did not say that each repetition produced a conscious experience. Say it anyway. The accounting is not in the feeling; it is in the saying.

Finally, as Ibn Taymiyyah frames it in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā: the servant's istighfār is itself a sign that Allah has already turned toward him. Only the one Allah has decided to receive is given the tawfīq to ask to be received. The dua is at once the request and the evidence that the request has already been heard. One says it as petition. One should also hear it as mercy.
